sheets.title: Executive Overview
sheets.headline:
What this is, why we prepared it,
and what it does not claim.

blocks.text: One page of orientation before any numbers. We built this from your public filings before contacting you, because a useful conversation should begin with evidence rather than a capability presentation.

blocks.label: What the public record lets us model today
paras: $9.7M a year recovered from what you currently pay suppliers, across six categories of indirect spend. Not a range. The median outcome across 533 completed ERA engagements in the six categories below — operating supply, uniforms and linens, small parcels, payroll and HR, fleet, insurance.
$6.0M a year on our weakest quartile. 1,913 of 2,468 completed engagements recovered value — and some returned nothing.

This is the visible starting point, not the limit of the work. ERA examines every applicable category using your contracts, invoices and operating requirements, including categories a Form 990 cannot separate or does not report at all.

sheets.title: What we found, and what follows
sheets.headline:
Five things stood out.
None of them is a conclusion.

blocks.text: A short summary of what our reading suggested and why each section is here, so you can decide how much of the detail is worth your time.

items.eyebrow: What you buy is what you sell
items.heading: Your largest indirect line is not overhead. It is inventory.
paras: The biggest expense your filing breaks out apart from people is materials and supplies. In most organizations that line is small and administrative. In yours it is close to the work itself.
items.why: It means the usual assumption about this line is wrong, and we have said so before quoting anything.
items.how: Separate resale inventory from consumed supply, identify the buying relationships behind the line, and establish the addressable baseline before any recommendation is made.

items.eyebrow: Your filing names its own suppliers
items.heading: Three relationships are stated in your own words, with amounts.
paras: Part VII Section B asks for the highest-paid contractors, what each was engaged to do and what each was paid. Yours describes the service. Most filings say less.
items.why: It lets us speak about specific arrangements rather than about categories in general.
items.how: Use the disclosed relationships as starting points, then test contract structure, pricing, service levels and alternatives with the relevant category specialists.

items.eyebrow: The largest line is not the strongest evidence
items.heading: The category we can say most about is not the one with the most money in it.
paras: Depth of completed work and size of spend are different things, and here they do not point at the same category. We ordered what follows by evidence.
items.why: It is why the second section is not simply the second largest number.
items.how: Prioritize by evidence and feasibility, not simply by spend size, so management attention goes first to questions that can be answered credibly.

items.eyebrow: One line is a fifth of everything, and we left it alone
items.heading: The single biggest cost after people is reported in a way we will not model.
paras: It combines something we work with something we do not, in one figure, and your return is not required to separate them. We named it and stopped there.
items.why: What we decline to estimate tells you as much as what we estimate.
items.how: Break blended lines into their actual components using internal data, while refusing to assign value where the evidence does not support it.

items.eyebrow: The one question that could change the answer
items.heading: We do not know when any of this was last taken to market.
paras: Everything above describes structure. Whether it is competitive depends on something no filing records: when each arrangement was last tested, and against what.
items.why: If these were tested recently and held, this Report ends there — and that is a useful answer.
items.how: Establish when each arrangement was last tested, what the market was asked to provide, and whether the current outcome should be validated or challenged.

columns.heading: Why operating supply comes first
paras: At 19.4% of revenue against a 2.4% peer median it is roughly eight times, on 2,573 filers. A donated-goods retailer genuinely buys more supply than most nonprofits, so part of that gap is your model rather than your buying — how much is exactly the question. ERA has completed 69 operating-supply engagements at a median of 21%.

columns.heading: Why this is more than benchmarking
paras: A benchmark tells us where a question may exist. ERA's category specialists determine whether the difference is structural, contractual, operational or genuinely addressable — and help implement the answer.
The median is drawn from organizations that have mostly never market-tested these categories either. It describes what is normal, not what is available.

columns.text: Why the total is not the sum of the extremes

Six categories do not all land at the bottom of their range, or all at the top. The middle column adds each category at its own median, which is the outcome most likely to describe the set. The range beside it is the middle half, not the best and worst case.

We are not saying you are paying too much. We have not seen a contract, an invoice or a schedule of rates, and a filing cannot show whether a price is competitive. Sitting above a peer median is not overspending; it is a difference worth understanding.

blocks.text: FILED Form 990 Part IX and Part VII B, FY2024. Contractor names are held on file and are not printed. A line we declined to estimate is better shown than left out.
Priority 1 of 2

69 completed ERA engagements in this category. The middle half landed between 13.5% and 34.4%, at a median of 21.3% — $8.09M against your filed figure. It sits at the 98th percentile of 2,573 peers. That is the size of the question, not an estimate of what would be recovered here.
What we see
$37.97M reported as materials and supplies, the largest line on your return after people. At 19.4% of revenue against a peer median of 2.40%, it is the most distinctive position on the filing.
Why it matters

In most organizations this line is administrative and small. In yours it is close to the work itself. That does not make it inefficient — it makes it the line where a percentage point is worth more than anywhere else on the return.
What may be driving it

In our experience a supply line of this weight is usually several buying relationships reported as one figure, with different parts of the organization holding different pieces. That is category inference from completed work elsewhere, not a finding about you.
What we do not know

How many suppliers sit behind the line. Whether any of it is bought through a group purchasing arrangement. How much is resale inventory rather than consumed supply, which your return does not separate and which would change the answer materially.
What we would test first
The split between what is resold and what is consumed. Then the number of suppliers, and whether anyone in the organization sees the whole of it.

blocks.heading: How ERA would help
paras: 1. Separate resale inventory from supplies consumed in the operation.
2. Consolidate the supplier, item and location view so the full buying pattern is visible.
3. Normalize specifications and service requirements before comparing alternatives.
4. Test pricing, rebates, terms, fulfillment and supplier concentration with an operating-supply specialist.
5. Present options that preserve what works, support implementation of the approved choice, and measure the verified result. Current suppliers may remain.

paras: Priority 2 is not the second largest line. Small Parcels and Fleet are both bigger. It is here because 109 completed engagements is the second deepest evidence we hold, and because your own return states the service and the amount for it. Size does not earn a section; evidence does.

blocks.text: What we see

$1.52M paid to a single relationship your filing describes as laundry distribution. It is disclosed in Part VII Section B, which asks for your highest-paid contractors and what each was engaged to do.
Why it matters

Uniform and linen arrangements are among the longest-running contracts an organization holds. They renew quietly, the terms are rarely re-read, and the middle half of our completed work in this category ran from 16.2% to 42.2% — one of the widest spreads we see.
What may be driving it
A wide spread usually means the outcome depends less on the market than on how the agreement was structured and how long it has run. Category experience, not something your filing shows.
What we do not know

When the arrangement was last tested. What the agreement covers beyond distribution. Whether the amount disclosed is the whole of what is spent on this service or only what went to the one relationship your filing names.
What we would test first
The contract term and the renewal mechanism, and whether the last renewal was a re-marketing or a rollover.

blocks.heading: How ERA would help
paras: 1. Read the agreement, amendments, renewal language and service schedule.
2. Reconcile invoices to contracted rates, quantities, replacements, losses, minimums and ancillary charges.
3. Validate the service model by location and user requirement.
4. Compare the complete commercial structure — not only the unit price — with relevant alternatives.
5. Negotiate or redesign the arrangement approved by Goodwill, support the transition if one is needed, and verify the result after implementation.

blocks.takeaway: The opportunity depends on contract architecture and invoice reality, not on obtaining a competing quote.

sheets.title: What happens next
sheets.headline: A conversation. That is the whole of the ask.

blocks.text: There is no proposal in this document and no scope of work. The next step is replacing what we assumed with what you know.

items.heading: A conversation
paras: We walk the operating supply question together and you tell us what the filing could not: how much of it is resale, and who buys it.
items.why: Costs you: the time it takes.

items.heading: A no-cost baseline
paras: If it is worth going further, we replace what we have inferred with your actual contract data — across every applicable category, not only the six shown.

items.heading: A category-by-category action plan
paras: Our specialists validate the facts, explain which arrangements should remain, and present practical options for the categories where action is justified.
items.why: Costs you: nothing, and nothing changes without your approval.

items.heading: Implementation and verified recovery
paras: For the actions you approve, ERA supports negotiation, implementation and measurement so identified value becomes an operating result rather than a recommendation left on a shelf.
items.why: Costs you: a share only of verified recovery, after you receive it.

outcomes: An independent read you can stand behind.
Recovered, measured, and only then charged for.

blocks.takeaway: The path is low risk and useful even when no change is recommended — it branches only at the end, and both endings are real results.

columns.heading: And if the answer is no
paras: If a current arrangement is already competitive, we will say so and show why. Independent validation is a useful result. Where value is verified, we help capture it. In either case, Goodwill keeps control of every decision.
Our fee: a share of what is actually recovered, after you have it. No recovery, no fee.

columns.heading: Every figure is live online
paras: Change any assumption and the model moves with it — and if we have read something wrongly, the page will record your correction as yours.

blocks.text: Some of it may prove accurate. Some of it may not. That is not the point. The purpose of this Report is not to prove an estimate. It is to work out — using your own contracts and data — whether opportunity genuinely exists, and to tell you honestly when it does not.

Aligned economics. No verified recovery means no fee.

args.title: What ERA brings, end to end
args.note: Breadth and execution. The Brief is the beginning of the work, not the whole of it.

blocks.takeaway: ERA brings both the breadth to see the whole portfolio and the execution to turn the right findings into an operating result.

paras: What we found in the filing is the beginning of the work. The value ERA brings is knowing where else to look, how to test each category, and how to turn the right findings into dollars that stay closer to mission.

blocks.text: We recommend keeping incumbents whenever they are the right choice. The objective is not changing suppliers. You remain in complete control — nothing changes without your approval, ever.
